records.name: Old-School Essentials: Designing a Dungeon
mappingNotes: The dungeon setting determines the structure of rooms and connecting passages.
Typically, dungeon maps are drawn on graph paper with a 10-foot per square scale.
Number each area so the map can be cross-referenced with its contents.
Stock important monsters, treasures, and story areas first; use the random table for areas of less importance.
Deeper dungeon levels should generally have greater risks and rewards. Normally, 1 HD monsters live on the 1st level, 2 HD on the 2nd, and so on.
For experienced players, place very few completely unguarded treasures. The referee may wish not to place any unguarded treasures on the 9th or deeper levels.

guidance.monsters: May be selected by hand or rolled on an encounter table.
guidance.specials: Weird or magical features of an area, including tricks or puzzles.
guidance.traps: If treasure is present, the trap may be set so that it is triggered when the treasure is tampered with (a treasure trap). Otherwise, the trap may be triggered by simply entering the room or a certain area of it (a room trap).
guidance.treasure: If a monster is in the room, roll the treasure type indicated in its description. Otherwise, the treasure depends on the dungeon level.

exampleRoomTraps.name: Falling block
exampleRoomTraps.description: Inflicts 1d10 damage (save versus petrification to avoid).

exampleRoomTraps.name: Gas
exampleRoomTraps.description: Poisonous gas fills the room (save versus poison or die).

exampleRoomTraps.name: Pit
exampleRoomTraps.description: Opens up beneath characters' feet, inflicting falling damage on any who fall in.

exampleRoomTraps.name: Scything blade
exampleRoomTraps.description: Swings from the ceiling, attacking for 1d8 damage.

exampleRoomTraps.name: Slide
exampleRoomTraps.description: Opens up beneath characters' feet, sending them to a lower level.

exampleTreasureTraps.name: Darts
exampleTreasureTraps.description: 1d6 spring-loaded darts fire at the character, doing 1d4 damage each.

exampleTreasureTraps.name: Flash of light
exampleTreasureTraps.description: Causes blindness for 1d8 turns (save versus spells).

exampleTreasureTraps.name: Hidden monster
exampleTreasureTraps.description: e.g., a snake; released when the treasure is disturbed.

exampleTreasureTraps.name: Illusion
exampleTreasureTraps.description: Typically of a monster. The monster has AC 9 [10] and vanishes if hit in combat. Its attacks do not inflict real damage: a PC who appears to die just falls unconscious for 1d4 turns.

exampleTreasureTraps.name: Spray
exampleTreasureTraps.description: A mysterious liquid covers the character. Monsters are attracted to the smell: the chance of wandering monsters is doubled for 1d6 hours.

exampleTreasureTraps.name: Sprung needle
exampleTreasureTraps.description: A needle coated with poison jabs out (save vs. poison or die).

exampleSpecials.name: Alarms
exampleSpecials.description: Entry alarm that attracts nearby guardians.

exampleSpecials.name: Animating objects
exampleSpecials.description: Inanimate objects that attack if disturbed.

exampleSpecials.name: Falling blocks
exampleSpecials.description: Stone block falls to prevent passage.

exampleSpecials.name: Shifting architecture
exampleSpecials.description: Doors lock, and the room rotates, rises, or falls.

exampleSpecials.name: Strange waters
exampleSpecials.description: Pool or fountain with weird, magical effects.

exampleSpecials.name: Teleports
exampleSpecials.description: Magical portal or teleporter to another area of the dungeon.

exampleSpecials.name: Voices
exampleSpecials.description: Walls or architectural features speak or moan (e.g., a talking statue).
